attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his Substack post. It is not a quotation of anyone else.

semantics.note: The normalised wording matches the source word for word and keeps the scope 'LLMs that lack explicit models'. It is unhedged ('is literally'), so it is scorable as a causal risk claim.

contract.note: The plain reading treats the sentence as a practical safety warning: delegating life-critical decisions to these chatbots exposes people to life-threatening errors. That is an ordinary reading. It does not require deaths or proof of the mechanism, and treating 'lack explicit models' as scope rather than a proven cause is fair. Whether the claim is supported depends on this reading.

evidence.note: A peer-reviewed study from 2024, before the post. Emergency physicians found dangerous content in 5–35% of answers from four consumer chatbots, including incomplete or wrong advice on when to seek urgent care. This is independent evidence of life-relevant risk from relying on them.

A 2025 vignette study in which GPT-4 helped physicians make better chest-pain decisions. This was assisted use, not delegation. It does not show that leaving decisions to LLMs is safe, so it does not contradict the claim.

reviews.rationale: The plain reading is that leaving life-critical decisions to these chatbots exposes people to danger. e1, independent and peer-reviewed, found dangerous advice and omissions about life-threatening conditions across the major chatbots, which meets the support condition. e2 shows benefit only when physicians use the model as an aid, which the contract excludes as a contradiction. The packet does not test whether the lack of explicit world models causes the failures, and the contract does not require that.
